data.title: Live updates: Trump telerallies planned in 19 states; Atlanta G20 meeting continues after early tensions
data.description:
President Trump is slated to speak at telerallies across the country Saturday, marking his last scheduled campaign appearance in several key battlegrounds before Election Day next week.

Trump is set to appear in virtual events in at least 19 states — Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia. The rallies will run at 4 p.m., 4:30 p.m. and 5 p.m. EDT.

The Republican National Committee first announced these telerallies Thursday after Trump canceled two in-person appearances in Kansas and Iowa — a move he walked back the next day. The president said during a Friday night rally in Daytona Beach, Fla., individuals from the two states called him and said, “We just want to make sure that we win.”

“I thought this was it. I thought I could relax. 28 days in a row of this crap is a lot. It’s a lot. My voice is about operating at about 49.2 percent,” Trump said Friday. “And then they called me in Iowa, and they called me in Kansas, and they said, ‘Sir, would it be possible to do a little rally of about 50,000 people each?'”

Meanwhile, Group of 20 diplomats will convene in Atlanta for the second day of its annual Foreign Ministers’ meeting. The gathering got heated on its first day, with its U.S. hosts deciding not to carry out the “family photo” tradition after several members refused to appear in a picture alongside a Russian official due to his country’s war in Ukraine.

Follow live below.

data.title: What a diploma measures when A's are the new normal
data.description:
Early decision applications are going out this fall, most of them due by mid-November, and the families sending them are committing to a very large bill. What they receive at the end of four years is a transcript and a diploma, and it is fair to ask what those two documents now report. 

Two issues answer the question, and they run in opposite directions. 

The first is grades. Stuart Rojstaczer and Christopher Healy collected grading records from American colleges and universities going back to 1940. In 1960, they found, C was the most common grade in the country, and D’s and F’s together outnumbered A’s. In their latest data, from the late 2000s, the A was the most common grade, at about 43 percent of all letter grades. That is 28 percentage points higher than in 1960, which means the A had nearly tripled its share. 

The most selective schools have gone furthest. By Harvard’s own count, A’s made up 24 percent of all grades awarded in 2005, 40 percent in 2015 and 60 percent in 2025.

Princeton tried to hold the line. In 2004 it told every department to hold A-range grades to less than 35 percent. Ten years later its faculty voted the limit away, after years of student complaints that it hurt them against applicants from schools with no such limit. Princeton’s own review found no measurable harm, but the perception was enough. Once most schools inflate, a school that grades honestly looks as though it is penalizing its own graduates, and few institutions will bear that cost for long.

Harvard is about to test that: In May, its faculty voted 458 to 201 to limit A’s to 20 percent of each course’s enrollment plus four students, starting in the fall of 2027. 

The second issue is effort, and it fell. Philip Babcock and Mindy Marks assembled half a century of time-use surveys. Full-time students in 1961 put about 40 hours a week into class and studying. By 2003, the figure was about 27 hours. The authors found the decline broad-based and not easily explained by students working more, choosing different majors or changes in who was enrolling. Over the same decades in which the A nearly tripled, the work behind it fell by about a third. 

Direct tests of learning cover a shorter span but point the same way. Richard Arum and Josipa Roksa followed students at more than two dozen four-year colleges as they took the Collegiate Learning Assessment in 2005, 2007 and 2009. After four years, 36 percent showed no significant improvement.

That is one cohort in one decade, not a 50-year trend. Still, it is the wrong result for anyone who would defend the grading record by arguing that students simply got better. If the A of 2008 stood for more learning than the A of 1960, students should have been working more and testing better. They were working less, and more than a third finished college testing about where they started. 

The consequences reach well beyond campus, because a grade is a piece of information, and so is a degree. Bryan Caplan and other economists who study signaling argue that much of a degree’s value comes from what it tells an employer about the holder: that he is reasonably able, conscientious and willing to finish what he starts.

Such a signal is worth something only while it is scarce. When few people held degrees and few grades were A’s, both told an employer something. When nearly everyone can send the signal, it stops sorting anyone, and what the employer is left reading is noise. 

Employers respond the way any buyer of information would. They ask for a bachelor’s degree for jobs most current holders do without one, and they lean on other proxies, such as the prestige of the school or a personal connection. Each student who buys the credential is acting sensibly for himself, but taken together, the whole population pays more for a signal that tells less, and no one ends up ahead. 

None of this calls for a federal grading standard or a mandated curriculum. The four-year degree bundles at least three different things. One is real skill, which could be delivered by shorter, rigorous programs in specific fields. Another is the signal, which could be supplied by portable certifications that employers assess for themselves. The third is a few years of growing up, which apprenticeships, service and work can also provide. 

The bundle survives because most of the federal student aid is attached to it, and the institutions selling it have every incentive to keep the pieces together. Take away the subsidy that props up the bundle, let the pieces compete on their own, and the diploma will have to start measuring something again or else lose its customers. 

Families writing checks this fall are paying dearly for a transcript on which the top grade has become the ordinary one. They deserve to know what they are buying. 

Jeffrey Janik is the author of “University for All: A Societal Disaster.”

data.title: DOJ pushes to isolate Alaska ballots in Peltola probe
data.description:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) pushed to isolate some Alaska ballots as part of a probe into whether the presence of two candidates with the same name could confuse voters in the state, a Friday court filing shows.

The investigation centers around reporting by The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign recruited a man with the same name as her Republican opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), to enter Alaska’s Senate race and potentially confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign has denied any involvement.

Now, the DOJ is requesting any ballots which rank Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., the other candidate, to be separated out as part of the investigation.

“There is a substantial risk that Mr. Sullivan’s sham candidacy will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity,” the court filing reads. “To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion.”

Sen. Dan Sullivan is denoted as the incumbent and a registered Republican on the ballot. President Trump claimed that Alaska voters “don’t know what incumbent means,” while some Alaska voters who spoke to CNN said that there is no confusion, and that the controversy may not impact their vote.

The department is investigating whether the alleged ballot stacking effort broke the law, and the U.S. attorney on the case confirmed that there has been a “surge of law enforcement” to Alaska as part of the investigation.

The DOJ had previously sued to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if the Sen. Sullivan loses, a move which legal and election experts said had no basis in court.

Scott Kendall, an Alaska lawyer and former GOP operative, previously told The Hill that if Peltola’s campaign did engage in ballot stacking, the move would be wrong, but not in violation of the law.

“These allegations don’t make the Department of Justice’s case a better case,” Kendall said. “There’s no basis for this lawsuit.”

With just a few days remaining until the election, the DOJ asked the judge to expedite their request and segregate the ballots prior to the election.

“These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration,” the court filing reads.

Alaska, given its size and large rural population, is a primarily vote-by-mail state, thus ballots can take several days to arrive after the election.

Elections in the state also utilize ranked choice voting, which allows voters to rank their preferences, and votes are reallocated to other candidates should no one receive a majority of the vote in the first round. That tabulation does not take place until more than two weeks after Election Day, once all mail-in ballots have been received.

Peltola is still a slight favorite to win the Senate race, according to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, which gives her a 60 percent chance of victory.

data.title: El-Sayed accuses Stevens of 'relitigating' primary after calls for apology on Israel
data.description:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) is firing back on his former primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), after she expected him to apologize over his comments on Israel just a few days out from the high-stakes Michigan Senate race.

Stevens said would appear alongside El-Sayed for the first time since their August primary this weekend but criticized him over his response to a controversial anti-Israel ad that appeared to link the country to high U.S. grocery prices.

“So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed said in a statement posted to the social platform X.

Support for Israel was a focal point of the widely watched Senate primary, with Stevens backed by millions from pro-Israel lobbying groups.

Since the primary, Stevens has supported El-Sayed and endorsed him immediately after. But Stevens’s fiancé, who is Jewish, recently said he would vote for former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers over El-Sayed.

Stevens reaffirmed that she would support El-Sayed in a CNN interview on Wednesday but said some Michigan voters are “hurt” and “confused” about the ad linking Israel to grocery prices.

She said in a statement on Friday that El-Sayed did not denounce the ad forcefully enough and expected him to apologize.

“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

Rogers has courted disaffected Democrats, mainly Jewish voters, as part of his effort to win Michigan in a Democratic-leaning year.

Stevens said she accepted an invitation from Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.), a major leader in the Black and Christian communities, to appear alongside the congressman and El-Sayed in a Detroit church service on Sunday.

The Hill reached out to both Stevens and El-Sayed to see if the joint appearance will continue as planned.

data.title: Anna Eskamani is bringing the 'Mamdani Model' to Central Florida
data.description:
As the hours tick down to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Anna Eskamani continues her methodical, grassroots campaign for Orlando mayor in next year’s election. 

If Eskamani wins, progressive Democrats will have another municipal toehold in the largely red Sunbelt.

Numerous U.S. mayors and would-be mayors aspire to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s mantle, marketing themselves as “another Mamdani” or “the next Mamdani.” Term-limited after eight years in the Florida House of Representatives, Eskamani, 36, also hopes to replicate Mamdani’s victorious 2025 campaign, applying his organizational playbook.  

For Eskamani, a progressive Democrat and child of immigrants, a victory in the diverse 340,000-people resort city would culminate a nearly decade-long march. 

“Power matters only if you use it to make life better for people and close the gap between what people earn and what it costs to live here,” she said after Orlando magazine recently named her the third most powerful person in the city. “That’s the work I’ve done in Tallahassee, and it’s the work I’ll bring to City Hall.”

She is hardworking, upbeat and relentlessly optimistic, which energizes volunteers and supporters. By January 2026, her campaign had knocked on more than 33,000 Orlando doors and raised a $1.4 million war chest, mostly in small $50 and $100 donations.

“I’m definitely an optimist and believe there is good in people and that people can change, that you can persuade people,” she told me in a telephone interview.

Volunteer Elly Kennedy, 50, now a realtor, met Eskamani in the mid-2010s when both worked at Planned Parenthood. “She was a real hard-working woman in a field that wasn’t the easiest,” Kennedy said. “She always had smile on her face.” 

“I am a fan of her philosophy that we build from the ground up. It’s really a good feeling to have hope,” said Kennedy. 

Longtime Orlando Democratic political consultant and former Florida legislator Dick Batchelor was impressed when first encountering Eskamani in 2018: “Even then she had firm grasp of the legislative issues. She had basically prepared herself for the legislative race, unlike other first-time candidates.” 

Eskamani is both team player and insurgent. Even though she is not on this cycle’s ballot, she mobilized her network to canvas for Democratic turnout Nov. 3, and hosted a University of Central Florida candidate forum featuring Angie Nixon, a Senate hopeful who is affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, as well as more moderate statewide candidates. 

“She is very generous with her political capital,” said Batchelor. 

University of Central Florida political scientist Aubrey Jewett taught the undergraduate Eskamani and served on her doctoral dissertation committee. “She is the kind of person that you want to help,” he recalled. “My first impression was that she was especially bright and energetic … [with] tremendous people skills.” 

As a mayoral candidate, he said “she has, as the young people say, the ‘rizz’ — charisma. She’s good at explaining things in a non-technical way. She has a magnetic personality and a compelling personal story. … She is very positive and optimistic and hopeful.” 

Eskamani was one of 48 first-time women candidates pictured on a 2018 Time magazine cover. The New York Times featured her as well. She was also featured in a prescient profile in The Atlantic by David Graham, complete with her smiling photo, headlined, “Hundreds of progressive, state-level candidates running in 2018 could pull the Democratic Party leftward for years to come.” 

“If Eskamani beats her Republican opponent in November,” Graham wrote in 2018, “she’ll join a class of progressive candidates whose elections will reshape the Democratic Party. … Once in office, they will pull the Democratic Party leftward for years to come.” 

And so she has, winning her initial legislative race — endorsed by Barack Obama, Orlando Mayor Buddy Dyer and the state AFL-CIO — and then reelected three times by healthy margins, until term-limited this year. 

Mamdani and Eskamani do have differences, however. 

Eskamani eschews ideological labels and is not a Democratic Socialists of America member. She supports a two-state Israel/Palestine solution but characterizes the Israeli war in Gaza as genocide. She recognizes the latter position creates “a difficulty for my Jewish brothers and sisters.” 

Unlike Mamdani, Eskamani has had few campaign trail questions on the divisive issue, which has bedeviled numerous other Mamdani wannabes. 

Growing up in working-class circumstances deeply affected Eskamani’s progressive politics. Her immigrant parents fled Iran separately as teenagers, Baha’i faith members, and met in Orlando. Their mother’s cancer death when she was 13 deeply impacted Anna. 

“I had a very challenging but loving childhood,” she recalls. “I grew up watching my parents work multiple jobs just to keep up, and too many families here are living that same story right now.” 

“Deep within me [lies] a source of focus and energy and determination” that comes from her parents, especially her mother, Eskamani said. “That was the unshakable core for me, the level of love she had for me.” 

Her father supported his University of Central Florida electrical engineering studies by table waiting and often left the country working for long periods during their youth. Later he worked weekends as a Disney customer rep. 

In each campaign, she focuses on economics, jobs, health care, homelessness. She also champions the local gay and transgender community. Conventional wisdom is that her relentless campaigning has so far preempted the field for the 2027 mayoral election. 

How would Eskamani compare herself to Mamdani? 

“We are both happy warriors, both committed to our communities in New York and Orlando. We believe in mass public engagement as the most effective way to govern, and we believe that poverty is a policy issue.” 

Mark I. Pinsky is a journalist and author based in Durham, N.C.

data.title: Blackburn's move to governor leaves Hegseth with potential parachute
data.description:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s (R-Tenn.) bid to become Tennessee’s next governor is leaving a potential opening for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who is viewed as one of the top oversight targets in the next Congress if House Democrats take the majority. 

Hegseth, a former Army National Guard Major, is interested in the open Tennessee Senate seat, which expires in early 2031, two sources familiar with the matter told The Hill. A third source with knowledge of the conversations said Hegseth is campaigning behind the scenes for the post. A fourth who works closely with the Pentagon said his interest is an open secret. 

Questions are swirling inside the Pentagon over how long Hegseth lasts after the midterms even if he’s not impeached, according to two sources regularly in the building. 

The defense secretary is widely seen as one of the Iran war’s biggest boosters in the administration. That could become a liability if Republicans are left looking for people to blame after what polls suggest could be a painful midterms for the party, driven in part by the economic consequences of the war. 

Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson dismissed Hegseth’s interest in a move to the Senate as “beltway gossip by anonymous sources,” in a statement to The Hill. 

“Whoever is feeding you these claims are either badly misinformed or deliberately leading you astray to peddle Fake News,” she added. “Under President Trump’s leadership, Secretary Hegseth’s singular priority is leading the War Department and delivering on the President’s America First agenda.”

In 2022, the defense secretary purchased a home in Goodlettsville, Tenn., which is located around 15 miles north of Nashville. He previously ran for Senate in his home state of Minnesota in 2012, but didn’t win the Republican nomination. 

The Pentagon chief visited Tennessee earlier this month, stoking speculation about his future political ambitions. 

Hegseth traveled to the Volunteer State as part of the “Send Me Tour,” speaking to University of Tennessee’s ROTC Cadets, administering the oath of enlistment to new recruits and attending the University of Tennessee vs. University of Alabama football game, where he wore the school’s light-blue polo shirt with a Tennessee-orange longsleeve shirt underneath. 

“If there’s one entity that should win the Nobel Peace Prize every single year, it actually should be the United States military,” Hesgeth told recruits on Oct. 17 ahead of the football game. “Peace through strength: the reason our people live free, the reason we get to play football games like this one today, are because we are stronger than any other nation in the world.”

Blackburn, who is well ahead in the polls against her Democratic Party opponent Jerri Green, previously said that if she wins the gubernatorial race next week, she intends to stay in her seat until she is sworn in to pick her successor in the upper chamber. 

Some political observers in the state think Hegseth’s name recognition could help. 

“I certainly think Pete Hegseth is going to be the guy that is going to have the most weight in the room,” Tennessee GOP operative Monty Lankford told The Hill. “I mean, being the Secretary of War and having done what he’s done, and I’m confident [he would be] getting the endorsement of the president, I would think.” 

Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.), who has campaigned for Blackburn, has also thrown his name into the mix, along with former CoreCivic CEO Damon Hininger and Glenn Jacobs, the former mayor of Knox County. 

“I will be honored to have that,” Rep. Chuck Fleischmann (R-Tenn.), who is on the ballot for reelection in Tennessee’s 3rd Congressional District, said in a recent interview with Tennessee Lookout. 

Blackburn’s team said the senator is “squarely focused” on next week’s election and has not had any discussions about who “may replace her nor is there a ‘short list.’” 

“She has been very clear there will be no discussions about a potential replacement until the appropriate time,” campaign manager Abigail Sigler told The Hill in a statement. 

The chatter around Hegseth’s interest in the seat, which was noted earlier by Puck, comes as Democrats debate whether to try to impeach the Pentagon chief, and more broadly, how to bring oversight to the Iran war. 

Pentagon officials have defended the defense secretary, characterizing him as a “transformative leader” who instilled back standards and merit, leading to morale and recruitment inside the military to reach “all-time highs.”

“The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first,” Wilson said previously. 

Several House Democrats have told The Hill they back Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) impeachment salvo, which he publicized last month, and they would also back a Democrat-led push to force the defense secretary’s removal. 

The vote on Massie’s privileged resolution is expected to take place after lawmakers come back to Capitol Hill next month for the lame-duck session. 

House Democrats, including those on the House Armed Services Committee, have criticized Hegseth for the lethal attacks against alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, the Pentagon’s lack of transparency during the conflict with Iran and firing over a dozen senior military officers since taking office. 

The firings of respected military leaders has particularly rankled Republicans, who are also expressing growing frustration about Iran and Ukraine. 

Hegseth has argued the military branches are “rank-heavy” and out of touch with troops on the ground.

President Trump blasted Democrats on Thursday over their chatter about impeaching Hegseth, calling it “terrible. 

“All they do is they talk about impeaching everybody,” the president told reporters. “I mean, honestly, if we wanted to play that game, we could play it just as well. 

Trump again praised the Pentagon chief for doing a “great job” and being a “great warrior.”

But Hegseth’s standing on Capitol Hill is eroding, even as the Pentagon ramps up its push for an Iran war supplemental funding request, $350 reconciliation package, and a base Pentagon budget that tops $1.1 trillion. Some wonder if this could be the first time in more than 6 decades that Congress fails to pass the NDAA before the end of the year. 

“So much of it’s going to come down to how Iran is handled in the midterms? Are people losing their races over Iran, and as a result, is Trump looking for a scapegoat,” one source said, noting that Hegseth is someone who does want to spar with Democrats in hearings. 

If Trump ends up looking for a new defense secretary, the administration is struggling to decide who it should be, this source said. 

In the Senate, Democrats are quietly floating Hegseth’s ouster after the midterms, using the threat as leverage in defense spending talks with the White House, The Hill previously reported. The Democrats might have some Republican support.

data.title: New autism study complicates Trump administration's search for cause
data.description:
A recently published found associations between certain maternal health conditions during pregnancy and autism diagnoses across racial and ethnic groups, underscoring how much remains unknown as the Trump administration searches for a cause of autism.

Researchers from the New York University Grossman School of Medicine and the Kaiser Permanente School of Medicine published a study earlier this month that included 224 ,353 children born at Kaiser Permanente Northern California hospitals between 2010 and 2017. 

Out of the more than 200,000 children, 2.4 percent were diagnosed with autism — not too far off from the 3.2 percentage rate reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Across different racial and ethnic groups, autism rates generally hovered around 2 and 3 percent. 

But other findings stood out: Four out of 25 maternal health conditions — obesity, depressive episode, asthma and other maternal diseases complicating pregnancy — had a higher association with autism diagnoses when it came to white mothers than mothers who were Black, Hispanic or Asian and Pacific Islander. 

Magdalena Janecka, associate professor at the Grossman School of Medicine’s department of child and adolescent psychiatry and co-author of the study, said the research highlighted the need to further examine environmental factors. 

“I think this study highlights that the link between certain environmental factors and autism (and other conditions) is likely to be heterogeneous across different population groups: not because the fundamental biology differs, but because what these environmental factors entail may differ among different individuals,” Janecka said in written responses to The Hill. 

She emphasized that these findings are “definitely not” indicative that “these maternal conditions cause autism.” 

“Instead, it may indicate that some factors related to this maternal condition (e.g., genetic factors) are also implicated in autism. We still need to do more research to understand what exactly drives these effects,” she added. 

That conclusion is unlikely to satisfy the Trump administration, as some have set out on a mission to find the cause of autism.

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in April 2025 said the administration would determine the cause of rising autism rates by September of that year. When the deadline came around, he and President Trump speculated from the Oval Office that the common over-the-counter pain reliever acetaminophen taken during pregnancy could be linked to autism, without presenting new evidence. 

This claim was denounced by maternal medicine groups and autism advocates alike. A month later, Kennedy walked back this claim somewhat, saying there “is not sufficient to say it definitely caused autism, but it is very suggestive.” 

Kennedy has also long refused to discount the theory that vaccinations could be linked to autism, despite no evidence being found linking immunizations to later diagnoses. A CDC page published earlier this year claims “studies supporting a link have been ignored by health authorities.” 

The overarching position of groups like the nonprofit Autism Speaks is that autism spectrum disorder develops as a result of both genetic and environmental influences. This is a position that Janecka shares. 

“Our study neither supports nor challenges this,” said Janecka. “We don’t know what exactly drove the observations we reported, and so it is difficult to attribute them to either genetic or non-genetic factors.” 

In discussing their findings, researchers acknowledged that differences in access to care, insurance continuity, clinical follow-up and treatment patterns could have affected what they observed. 

An opinion piece published last year, co-authored by Janecka, argued differences in potential causes of childhood neuropsychiatric outcomes are “often overlooked,” with social determinants often filtered out of analyses. 

“As race/ethnicity is primarily a social construct—associated with experiences of structural inequities, racism, and environmental injustice—that aligns poorly with genetic ancestry, we emphasize that the differences in the exposure–outcome associations across race/ethnic strata would arise largely because of societal, rather than biological, causes,” the authors wrote. 

The study published this month took into account the history of underdiagnosis among certain groups, like the children of Black mothers being less likely to receive a diagnosis even when scoring high for autism-related traits in testing.  

According to experts, autism does not occur at different rates across different races and ethnicities. 

“We don’t have any evidence that shows that there’s any difference across race ethnicity in terms of autism diagnosis,” said Andy Shih, chief science officer of Autism Speaks.  

“We do see … racial, ethnic differences in terms of diagnosis between white kids and Asian kids and African American kids, Hispanic kids for example,” Shih added. “But you know those gaps have been closing. So, I think the latest report that we have — it actually shows that at least at national level that we have closed the gap in terms of some ethnicity-based assessment.” 

Shih hopes that the findings from the study bring more attention to the need for “the best healthcare access for expectant mothers.” 

Janecka added, “What I would hope our study highlights is the need for more studies like ours stratifying the observed effects by maternal race/ethnicity, as well as considering other ways to stratify the total population: based on e.g., insurance status. I think rather than regress some differences out of our models, we should strive to better understand them.” 

The Hill has reached out to HHS for comment.

data.title: Judge blocks DOJ from threatening election officials over noncitizen voting claims
data.description:
A California federal judge Friday ordered the Trump administration to stop threatening election officials with criminal prosecution in its ongoing efforts to crack down on noncitizen voting.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order connected to a lawsuit brought by unions representing California election workers earlier Friday. In her decision, the Biden-appointed judge noted Election Day was “around the corner.”

“Ballots have already been issued. Americans have already begun voting. Workers have already begun processing ballots,” Thompson wrote. “Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.”

The order also directs the Trump administration to halt its efforts to force these workers to remove certain people from voter rolls, deny ballot requests to some voters or set aside ballots for individuals it suspects are ineligible to vote.

The plaintiffs involved in this case include The Service Employees International Union; American Federation Of State, County and Municipal Employees; the League Of United Latin American Citizens and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. 

The initial complaint accuses Attorney General Todd Blanche and other top Justice Department (DOJ) officials of carrying out “a coordinated campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees.” 

This week, the DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states threatening potential prosecution if they failed to preserve election records. 

The DOJ had sent similar correspondence a week prior to election officials in every California county, demanding they work with the federal government to identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls. The letter warned these officials would “risk significant federal scrutiny” if they failed to comply with this request. 

Earlier this week, another federal judge in California threw out the Trump administration’s lawsuit attempting to require the state to set aside the ballots of 20,000 people the federal government had identified as potential noncitizens. A split federal appeals court panel upheld this ruling Friday. 

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ and the White House for comment on Thompson’s order.

data.title: Health insurance plan costs on Healthcare.gov to rise by double digits in 2027
data.description:
Obamacare enrollees could see their health insurance premiums rise by double digits for a second year in a row, according to a report published Friday.

Health research group KFF found the average cost of Obamacare health insurance will rise by 13 percent in 2027, following a 26 percent hike in rates from 2025 to 2026.

KFF made these calculations was based on new data the Trump administration shared earlier in the day, which listed 2027 prices for the 30 states with federal health insurance marketplaces. These new rates came ahead of the opening of the 2027 enrollment period on Sunday. 

Around 19.2 million Americans are enrolled in Obamacare plans, according to an estimate from the federal government earlier this year. A KFF analysis from May found that enrollment in this program fell in 2026 after four consecutive years of record growth. 

President Trump’s administration has implemented new barriers to enrolling in these programs as part of its efforts to crackdown on alleged widespread fraud. Earlier this year, Obamacare’s enhanced premium tax subsidies expired after Republican lawmakers opposed a Democrat-led push to extend them. 

Under the first Trump administration, Obamacare premium costs rose by an average of 20 percent in 2017 and 34 percent in 2018, according to KFF’s analysis. 

The estimated Obamacare premium cost increases for 2027 are similar to changes anticipated in other health insurance increases programs, with federal and employer plans expected to increase by around 10 percent in this timeframe. 

Health care costs have become a key issue in the midterm elections, as the rising cost of living continues to poll highest among the top concerns motivating Americans’ votes in this election. 

A KFF survey published earlier this month found six in 10 voters said they were concerned about being able to afford their health insurance and out-of-pocket medical bills. Respondents ranked health care costs on par with gas prices as the most important affordability issue this election cycle. 

The Trump administration has sought to address these concerns ahead of Election Day. The president announced the federal government would disburse one-time $500 checks to nearly 1 million Americans the administration said were overcharged for Obamacare.

Earlier this month, the administration also began sending out $90 each to over 20 million seniors enrolled in Medicare Part B — totaling around $2 billion. 

Democrats have vowed to make restoring Obamacare subsidies and health care tax credits a top issue if they regain control of Congress.

The State Department approved on Friday a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine that is funded entirely by U.S. partners and allies. 

© Getty

The Trump administration greenlit the sale of 500 PATRIOT Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) missiles, including classified and unclassified spare parts

 

“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the State Department said in the press release. 

 

Ukraine will pay for the purchase with donations from Norway, Germany and Canada via the JUMPSTART program and national funds. No U.S. funds are involved in the transaction. 

 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Patriot missile interceptors are paramount to shooting down Russian missiles and drones targeting the country’s cities. 

 

Zelensky has previously accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of missile interceptors that other nations bought for Kyiv. 

 

“We have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS,” Zelensky said this week. 

 

Two weeks ago, Hegseth told reporters that the Pentagon has not changed its posture toward Ukraine, but noted that “we want to make sure our guys have the most possible” interceptors.
